While I agree that the end of the Space Race left the American public without a clear competitive objective to rally around, I think that post-Apollo NASA failed to devise or cultivate any sort of coherent civil space development paradigm or space industrial logistics infrastructure as an alternative. The creation of a civilian space program was premised on the opening of space to society. After you plant the flags, you build the highways. NASA had an obligation to cultivate the kind of space infrastructure and orbital industrial research that would lead to commercial/entrepreneurial development. But government interest in this was always insincere (governments simply aren't in the business of inventing new places for people to go and not pay taxes...) and NASA's 'mission' became increasingly focused on it's own self-perpetuation as a venue for pork. For me the turning point was when the original planning for the space station changed, with the finalization of the Shuttle design, from a telerobot-built logistics facility intended to extend our reach into the solar system into a nebulously defined multinational space lab in a logistically useless orbital location. The Shuttle and ISS became co-dependent White Elephants by design. (remember when it was supposed to have a dual keel space frame with construction and service hangars and a modular reusable inter-orbital/cis-lunar space tug? We were going to build stuff and go places)

What frustrates me about NASA today is its persistently retrofuturist outlook. Every concept we see today from space agencies, New Space moghuls, and the remnant space advocacy movement are all re-hashes of 30-60 year old ideas. Space futurism is generally decades behind the curve of the rest of futurism, always neglecting the trends apparent in contemporary technology, because--I suspect--we fear the logical conclusions that leads to and which run contrary to our personal fantasies of space adventure. The conclusion that human beings are not doing the heavy lifting in space. The conclusion that, if space is a competition for cost-efficiency, humans already lost. The conclusion that the only practical role for humans in space is in competition with machine intelligence as a solution to telecommunications latency. The conclusion that spacecraft like Progress/Orion/Dragon are probably about all we're likely to actually need in manned spaceflight capability for the foreseeable future. The conclusion that the only point left for humans to go there is to live there, if that's at all possible. A lifestyle choice that has to realize it's ROI out there rather than on Wall Street through a model of The Good Life in space we've yet to imagine. The conclusion that we've squandered so much time that the long-term future in space may already belong to a transhuman culture--to 'people' who can travel by telecommunications and live off solar and nuclear power. I think there's a kind of epiphany on the horizon akin to that of oceanographer Bob Ballard's when he first began working with underwater ROVs and realized the era of the manned deep sea submersible was over. But there is a great opportunity in this. A potential for global and personal participation that was not possible in the past and which remains overlooked. We're entering an era where everyone can have a space program as long as they're willing to change their POV about what a space program is and is for. But, we're still talking about billion dollar camping trips and planting flags rather than infrastructures.
